strengths: The paper proposes a genuinely unifying analytical lens (TPV, with trace form Tr(Heff C)) that connects several previously disparate phenomena — label noise, SGD stationary noise, quantization noise, and pruning — under a single curvature-covariance decomposition, which is a conceptually appealing contribution.

Theorem 2.1 (TPV Trace Stability) is proven rigorously in the appendix using NTK stability and LLN arguments, and represents (to the reviewer's knowledge) a novel result showing training-set prediction-variance estimates can approximate test-set prediction variance under local perturbations, independent of the generalization gap.

Empirical validation is extensive: 324+324 synthetic configurations spanning widths, depths, dataset types and noise sources, plus CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet experiments, consistently confirming TPV stability and its correlation with test loss across very different architectures (including extremely narrow networks).

The paper is unusually careful and honest about the limits of its own theory: Appendix C.2 explicitly walks through pathological/degenerate regimes (interpolation, large noise, low n_train) where TPV stability trivializes or breaks, which strengthens the paper's scientific credibility rather than overselling the theorem.

The JBR pruning criterion derived from the TPV framework is a natural, well-motivated practical application, and is shown to be competitive with or better than several established pruning baselines (L1, FPGM, BN-scale, WHC, Taylor, Jacobian criterion) on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet without fine-tuning.

Reproducibility is good: experimental protocols, hyperparameters, and practical caveats (eval-mode training, fixed mini-batch order, first-order validity checks via finite differences) are documented in detail in the appendix.
weaknesses: There is a notable gap between theory and the most striking empirical finding: Theorem 2.1 requires the NTK (infinite-width) regime, yet the paper's headline empirical result is that TPV stability holds even at width=1, which the theory does not explain (the authors acknowledge the theorem may be sufficient but not necessary, which somewhat undercuts the explanatory power of the main theoretical contribution).

JBR, the practical pruning method, is explicitly presented as "a label-free version of" the existing Jacobian Criterion (JC) of Chen et al. (2025), differing only in substituting predicted labels for ground-truth labels; the technical novelty of this contribution is therefore incremental relative to prior work.

Several of the perturbation-specific derivations (SGD noise Theorem 3.3, quantization Remark 3.4) rely on multiple heuristic approximations (dropping an O(1/n^2) term, assuming squared residuals are i.i.d. and independent of Jacobian geometry) that are not tightly justified theoretically, and their validity is asserted rather than empirically stress-tested in the main paper (the authors explicitly state they omit SGD/flatness experiments, deferring to prior literature).

The claimed "correlation between TPV and test loss" is demonstrated mainly through small-scale qualitative trend plots (a handful of widths or a handful of ImageNet architectures) rather than through systematic quantitative correlation statistics (e.g., correlation coefficients, larger architecture/dataset sweeps), limiting the strength of this claim.

The label-noise TPV computation is acknowledged to be numerically intractable for large networks (Appendix C.3.3), and the proposed workaround (local SGD with proximity regularization) is only an approximate proxy for the theoretical quantity, which weakens the direct empirical link between Theorem 3.2 and the reported CIFAR/ImageNet results.

Pruning experiments, while covering four settings, are relatively narrow in scope (no NLP/transformer models, no unstructured pruning, limited sparsity levels), and quantitative results are presented only as plots without tabulated numbers or statistical significance tests in the main text.

strengths: The paper proposes a conceptually appealing unifying quantity (TPV, Tr(Heff C)) that connects several previously disparate perturbation phenomena (label noise, SGD noise, quantization, pruning) under one trace-form template, and derives closed-form or approximate expressions for each case.

Substantial theoretical effort is put into the paper: a finite-sample NTK-stability-based proof of training/test TPV convergence (Appendix A), derivations for linear and non-linear label-noise TPV (Appendices B-C), and a derivation connecting SGD stationary noise and quantization noise to Hessian trace (Appendices D-E).

The empirical study is extensive, spanning synthetic data, CIFAR-10/100, and ImageNet, and includes ablations identifying the boundary conditions (sample size, noise magnitude) under which TPV stability holds or breaks, which is a genuinely interesting empirical observation.

The proposed pruning criterion JBR is evaluated on four architecture/dataset combinations against several established baselines and shows competitive performance, providing at least one concrete practical use case for the framework.
weaknesses: A central advertised result (Theorem 2.1 / TPV trace stability) is proved only in the infinite-width NTK regime, yet the paper's headline empirical finding is that stability holds even at width=1 (Fig. 1), which is explicitly outside the regime the theorem covers. The authors acknowledge this gap ("the former condition is hardly required... this leads us to believe Theorem 2.1 may be a sufficient condition... but not necessary") but never provide an alternative theoretical account for why stability holds at such extreme widths, leaving the core claim essentially unexplained rather than proven.

The theoretical derivations rely on a long chain of successive approximations (first-order Taylor linearization, dropping an O(1/n^2) term, assuming residual magnitudes are independent of Jacobian geometry, neglecting O(eta^2) terms in the SGD Lyapunov argument, assuming Heff ≈ Hessian only in a vague 'small-loss regime'), none of which come with quantitative error bounds. The cumulative effect of these approximations on the final claimed formulas (Thm 3.2, 3.3, Remark 3.4) is never assessed, so it is unclear how tight or reliable these expressions actually are outside toy settings.

The trace-stability bound in Theorem 2.1 scales with Tr(C), which the paper itself shows becomes vacuous/loose precisely in the regimes of practical interest (larger noise, Fig. 7, Appendix C.2 case 4), undermining the generality suggested in the abstract ("providing the first result that prediction variance... can be inferred from training inputs alone"). The paper's own pathological-case analysis (Appendix C.2) reveals that in several regimes TPV stability is either trivial/uninformative (interpolation regimes) or breaks down, narrowing the actually useful regime considerably relative to the claims made in the introduction.

The practical label-noise TPV estimation procedure (Appendix C.3) is admitted to be numerically intractable for deep networks (CG fails to converge, condition numbers of 10^6-10^8), and the paper falls back on a heuristic perturb-and-retrain SGD procedure that does not correspond to the exact minimum-norm solution analyzed theoretically. This weakens the connection between the theory (Theorem 3.2) and what is actually measured in the CIFAR/ImageNet experiments.

The flagship practical contribution, JBR pruning, is presented as nearly identical to the existing Jacobian Criterion (JC) of Chen et al. (2025), differing only in using predicted vs. ground-truth labels; the TPV framing is used post hoc to motivate an already-existing scoring formula rather than to derive a substantively new criterion, limiting the originality of this contribution.

The TPV-vs-test-loss correlation claims (Section 5.2, Figs. 5-8) are based on very small numbers of points (4-7 architectures/widths) without any reported correlation statistics (e.g., Pearson/Spearman coefficients, confidence intervals), making the 'TPV correlates well with clean test loss' claim largely qualitative and visually asserted rather than statistically substantiated.

The paper explicitly skips experiments on SGD-noise-driven flat-minima claims (Section 5), citing prior literature, despite SGD noise being one of the four headline perturbation sources in the framework; this leaves one of the paper's core theoretical contributions (Theorem 3.3) empirically unverified in the main experiments.

Overall presentation is dense and sprawling (32 pages with extensive appendices covering many special/pathological cases), which, combined with the unresolved theory-practice gap on the central stability claim, makes it difficult to assess how much of the paper's narrative is rigorously established versus suggestively argued.

strengths: Introduces a conceptually clean unifying quantity (TPV, with trace form Tr(Heff C)) that connects disparate phenomena -- SGD noise, label noise, quantization, and pruning -- under a single curvature-covariance framework, offering a fresh lens distinct from prior global bias-variance or NTK-based analyses.

Provides a rigorous theoretical result (TPV Trace Stability, Theorem 2.1/A.4) combining NTK stability and LLN arguments to show training-set TPV approximates test-set TPV in the overparameterized regime, which is a non-trivial and novel theoretical claim.

Derives closed-form TPV expressions for several concrete perturbation mechanisms (linear and non-linear label noise, SGD stationary noise, quantization noise), connecting these to established phenomena like benign overfitting and the wide-minima hypothesis in a unified way.

Extensive and carefully designed empirical validation across synthetic data, CIFAR-10/100, and ImageNet, spanning hundreds of configurations (widths, depths, data sizes, perturbation types), convincingly demonstrating TPV stability and its breakdown conditions.

Translates the theoretical framework into a practical, label-free pruning criterion (JBR) that is empirically competitive with or exceeds several established pruning baselines across CIFAR and ImageNet architectures.

Unusually transparent discussion of limitations and failure modes (e.g., Appendix C.2 on pathological/trivial regimes, C.3.3 on numerical intractability of exact Jacobian computations for deep nets), which strengthens the credibility of the claims rather than overselling them.
weaknesses: The central theoretical guarantee (Theorem 2.1) requires the infinite-width NTK regime, yet the most striking empirical finding is that stability holds even at width=1; the paper does not provide theoretical insight into why the bound is so loose/pessimistic relative to the much stronger empirical pattern, leaving a gap between theory and the main empirical message.

The flagship practical contribution (JBR pruning) is explicitly a label-free variant of the pre-existing Jacobian Criterion (Chen et al., 2025); the technical delta is a change of the reference vector m(x) from label-residual to predicted-class residual, which is a fairly small algorithmic modification despite being well-motivated by the TPV framework.

The paper explicitly notes that the TPV Trace Stability theorem does not apply to the scalar functional u(x;w) used in JBR, and defers this analysis to future work -- meaning the core theoretical result does not actually cover the paper's main showcased application.

Empirical validation of TPV under real SGD noise is omitted from the main experiments on the grounds that prior work has studied flat/sharp minima relationships, which weakens the completeness of the empirical story for one of the four motivating perturbation sources.

Practical estimation of the theoretical label-noise TPV object (via exact Jacobian SVD) is shown to be numerically intractable for deep networks (Appendix C.3.3), forcing reliance on a heuristic SGD-based proxy with several fragile practical requirements (eval-mode training, fixed mini-batch order, monitoring MSE convergence); for ImageNet, several architectures (MobileNetV2, DenseNet121, SqueezeNet) could not even be made to fit noisy logits, somewhat limiting the generality of the empirical pipeline.

Many of the core empirical claims are correlational (TPV correlating with test loss across widths/architectures) rather than demonstrating a tight quantitative or causal relationship, so the practical predictive utility of TPV for generalization remains suggestive rather than fully established.

The manuscript is very dense with numerous theorems, remarks, and extensive appendices; important caveats and nuances (e.g., the four regimes in Appendix C.2) are relegated to appendices, which may hinder a focused reading of the main paper's claims and could obscure the real scope of applicability of the theory.

strengths: Introduces a coherent unifying framework (TPV, trace form Tr(Heff C)) that connects several seemingly disparate phenomena—SGD noise, label noise, quantization, and pruning—under one first-order sensitivity lens, recovering known results (wide-minima hypothesis, benign overfitting) as special cases.

Provides a theoretical result (Theorem 3.1, TPV trace stability) with an explicit finite-sample proof (via NTK stability + LLN) showing training-set TPV approximates test-set TPV in the overparameterized regime, which is a genuinely novel justification for training-set-based robustness diagnostics.

Extends benign-overfitting-type analysis to nonlinear networks via Jacobian spectral geometry (Theorem 4.2), with careful discussion of pathological/degenerate regimes (interpolation, large noise) where the theory's assumptions break down—this honesty about limitations is a strength.

Extensive, carefully documented empirical verification across synthetic data, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, and even NLU tasks (BERT on AG News/TREC), demonstrating TPV stability holds far more broadly than the theorem requires (e.g., even at width=1), and correlates with test loss in a consistent (if regime-dependent) way.

Practical downstream applications are demonstrated: a label-free pruning criterion (JBR) that matches/exceeds several established baselines on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet, and four distinct training-set-only model-selection scenarios (in-distribution recipe selection, cross-architecture selection, transfer learning, and noise-robustness recipe selection), each with reasonably detailed experimental protocols.

The appendices are unusually thorough, including detailed proofs, discussion of computational intractability of exact label-noise TPV for deep nets, and a practical estimation algorithm with documented pitfalls (batch norm/dropout mode, mini-batch shuffling, loss convergence checks) that aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central stability theorem (3.1) relies on strong, somewhat unrealistic assumptions (isotropic perturbation covariance, infinite-width NTK stability) and yields a bound with an asymptotic constant c1 that is not shown to be numerically tight or predictive in any experiment; the theory is more suggestive than quantitatively validated.

Exact computation of label-noise TPV is admitted to be numerically intractable for real deep networks (Appendix D.3.3: CG fails to converge, condition numbers of 10^6-10^8); the paper instead relies on a heuristic 'perturb-and-retrain' estimator with several free hyperparameters (adaptive noise scale c, proximity regularization, learning rate, epochs) whose sensitivity is not systematically ablated, raising reproducibility concerns for the core practical quantity.

The empirical relationship between TPV and test loss (the U-shaped pattern underlying most 'applications') is purely empirical and not derived from the trace-form theory; the paper's own bias-variance decomposition (Eq. 3) does not predict this shape, so a key practical justification rests on observation rather than theory.

Cross-architecture model selection—one of the four headline applications—is explicitly reported to be noisier/less reliable than within-architecture selection (Figs. 10, 25) and the paper defers resolving this to future work, weakening the generality of the model-selection claims.

The proposed pruning method (JBR) is very close to an existing method (Jacobian Criterion, Chen et al. 2025), differing mainly in using predicted vs. ground-truth labels; the novelty here is somewhat incremental, and comparisons lack fine-tuning between pruning iterations, which may not reflect standard deployment pipelines.

Many empirical demonstrations use fairly small or subsampled datasets (e.g., 10k-image ImageNet subsets, small MLPs), and the breadth of settings, while extensive, sometimes trades depth for coverage—several key experiments (e.g., large-noise breakdown in Fig. 5, cross-architecture generalization) are only partially explained and left as open questions.

The paper's scope is very large (5 perturbation types, multiple theorems, multiple applications) which, combined with reliance on first-order/linearization approximations throughout, raises concerns about whether every individual claim received sufficiently rigorous testing versus being included for breadth.

strengths: The paper proposes a conceptually appealing unifying lens (Tr(Heff C)) that ties together several previously disparate phenomena (SGD noise, label noise, quantization, pruning) under a common local-sensitivity framework, and derives closed-form or asymptotic expressions for each source.

Extensive empirical verification of the central 'TPV stability' claim across synthetic data, CIFAR-10/100, and ImageNet, with many configurations (324 synthetic settings, multiple architectures/widths/sample sizes), including honest reporting of regimes where the phenomenon breaks (small n, large noise).

Two practical downstream applications (label-free pruning criterion JBR and training-set-only model selection across four deployment scenarios) are demonstrated, with JBR shown to be competitive with several established pruning baselines.

The appendix is unusually thorough, containing full derivations, a discussion of pathological/degenerate regimes for the label-noise theorem, and detailed experimental protocols that aid reproducibility.

The paper is reasonably transparent about limitations of its theory (NTK-regime assumptions, isotropic perturbation assumption, first-order approximation validity) and explicitly flags several open problems for future work.
weaknesses: The flagship theoretical result (Theorem 3.1, TPV trace stability) is proven under NTK-regime assumptions (infinite width, NTK kernel stability, isotropic perturbation covariance) that do not match the practical deep-learning settings (finite-width ResNets/MobileNets trained with SGD-momentum, batch norm, data augmentation, weight decay) in which the empirical experiments are actually run; the paper's own headline empirical finding that stability holds even at width=1 is in tension with -- rather than explained by -- the overparameterized/NTK-based theory, leaving a substantial unexplained gap between theory and observation that the paper itself acknowledges as future work rather than resolving.

The stability bound's scaling c1 = (ntr+nte)/p * εNTK + o(1) is not carefully analyzed with respect to the joint limit of n, m; it is unclear under what joint scaling of width and sample size the bound is actually informative, and no discussion is given of whether/how εNTK must shrink relative to n for the first term to vanish.

The practical label-noise TPV estimator used throughout Sections 5-6 (the 'perturb-and-retrain' heuristic in Appendix D.3.4) is explicitly acknowledged to not correspond to the theoretically derived minimum-norm solution of Theorem 4.2, and is introduced only because the exact linearized computation is numerically intractable for real networks (Appendix D.3.3, CG fails to converge). This means nearly all of the practical/empirical results in the paper validate a heuristic surrogate rather than the theorem being advertised as a core contribution, weakening the claimed link between theory and the paper's main practical applications.

The core quantity Tr(HeffC) is explicitly acknowledged by the authors to already appear in prior work (Zhu et al. 2018; Thomas et al. 2020; Bar et al. 2024); the paper's claimed novelty rests primarily on reinterpretation/unification rather than new mathematical machinery, which somewhat limits the technical originality of the contribution.

The derivations stack numerous simplifying assumptions (first-order Taylor linearization, minimum-norm stationary point assumption for label noise that need not match actual SGD/Adam solutions, dropping O(1/n^2) and O(eta^2) terms, residual-variance independence from Jacobian geometry) without a unified sensitivity analysis of how these compounding approximations affect the validity of the final claims.

The cross-architecture model-selection experiments (§6.2, transfer learning and ImageNet cross-architecture selection) are based on very small sample sizes (4-7 architectures, 5 configurations) and the paper itself notes that cross-architecture TPV correlations are 'noisier' and less reliable, undermining the practical robustness of one of the two headline applications.

Pruning results (§6.1, Appendix H) are presented only as accuracy-vs-MACs/percent-pruned curves without consolidated quantitative tables or significance testing, making it difficult to precisely assess whether JBR meaningfully outperforms or merely matches baselines.

The paper's empirical U-shaped TPV/test-loss relationship (§5.3) is presented as a purely empirical/post-hoc observation without a theoretical account of exactly when the correlation sign flips, limiting the predictive/diagnostic value of TPV as a principled model-selection tool beyond curve-fitting after the fact.

strengths: Conceptually appealing unifying framework: casting SGD noise, label noise, quantization, and pruning as instances of Tr(Heff C) provides a coherent lens connecting several previously separate literatures (wide-minima hypothesis, benign overfitting, NTK theory).

Substantial and careful theoretical development: the TPV trace-stability theorem (Thm 3.1) is proven rigorously via NTK stability + LLN arguments, and the label-noise theorem (Thm 4.2) cleanly generalizes the linear benign-overfitting result to nonlinear networks via Jacobian spectral geometry.

Extensive empirical validation across many settings (324 synthetic configurations, CIFAR-10/100 with varying width/architecture/dataset size, ImageNet, and even NLU tasks with BERT), consistently supporting the central empirical claim that TPV stability holds much more broadly than the theory strictly requires.

Honest and thorough discussion of failure modes and pathological regimes (Appendix D.2), including when TPV stability breaks (small n_train, large perturbations) and when the label-noise TPV becomes uninformative (interpolation regimes) — this transparency strengthens the credibility of the claims.

Practical utility is demonstrated via two concrete applications: a label-free pruning criterion (JBR) that is competitive with strong baselines, and training-set-only model-selection diagnostics validated across four deployment scenarios (in-distribution recipe/architecture selection, transfer learning, and label-noise robustness recipe selection).
Very detailed appendices with proofs, algorithmic details (e.g. the perturb-and-retrain TPV estimator), and extensive experimental protocols, which substantially aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: The gap between the formal theorem (Theorem 3.1, which requires NTK stability, isotropic perturbations, and the overparameterized limit) and the much broader empirical stability claimed (including at width=1) is large and not fully explained theoretically; the paper acknowledges this as future work but the current theoretical support for the central empirical finding is thin.

The practical label-noise TPV estimator (Appendix D.3.4) is a heuristic perturb-and-retrain procedure that does not provably correspond to the exact minimum-norm linearized solution analyzed in Theorem 4.2 (CG fails to converge for deep nets), so the link between the theory and what is actually measured in most experiments remains approximate and not tightly characterized.

JBR, the proposed pruning criterion, is explicitly noted to be very close to the existing Jacobian Criterion (JC, Chen et al. 2025), differing only in using predicted vs. ground-truth labels; this makes the pruning contribution somewhat incremental rather than a clearly novel method, and the empirical gains are described as matching rather than consistently exceeding baselines.

Several derivations (SGD-noise TPV, quantization TPV) rely on a chain of approximations (dropping O(1/n^2) terms, assuming residual/geometry independence, small-loss/local-Hessian approximations) whose validity conditions are not rigorously bounded, weakening the precision of the stated theorems (they read more as informal derivations despite being labeled 'Theorem').

Key hyperparameters in the empirical TPV estimation pipeline (adaptive noise scale c, σ0, proximity regularization) appear to be tuned per experiment without a principled selection procedure, raising concerns about robustness/reproducibility of the quantitative comparisons across architectures.

Cross-architecture model-selection results are explicitly acknowledged by the authors to be noisier/weaker than within-architecture results, limiting the practical reach of one of the paper's main claimed applications.

The paper is very dense, with many essential results, proofs, and experimental details relegated to a lengthy appendix, which can make the main text feel like a high-level summary that depends heavily on appendix material to fully substantiate central claims.
